title: The charge of magic learned in Egypt
source_text: Ἔτι δὲ λαβὼν ἀπὸ τῆς γεγραμμένης ἐν τῷ κατὰ Ματθαῖον εὐαγγελίῳ ἱστορίας περὶ τοῦ εἰς Αἴγυπτον ἀποδεδημηκέναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν τοῖς μὲν παραδόξοις εἰς τοῦτο οὐκ ἐπίστευσεν, οὔθ᾿ ὅτι ἄγγελος τοῦτο ἔχρησεν, οὔτε εἴ τι ᾐνίσσετο ὁ καταλιπὼν τὴν Ἰουδαίαν Ἰησοῦς καὶ Αἰγύπτῳ ἐπιδημῶν· ἀνέπλασε δέ τι ἕτερον. συγκατατιθέμενος μέν πως ταῖς παραδόξοις δυνάμεσιν, ἃς Ἰησοῦς ἐποίησεν, ἐν αἷς τοὺς πολλοὺς ἔπεισεν ἀκολουθεῖν αὐτῷ ὡς Χριστῷ, διαβάλλειν δ᾿ αὐτὰς βουλόμενος ὡς ἀπὸ μαγείας καὶ οὐ θείᾳ δυνάμει γεγενημένας· φησὶ γὰρ αὐτὸν σκότιον τραφέντα, μισθαρνήσαντα εἰς Αἴγυπτον, δυνάμεών τινων πειραθέντα ἐκεῖθεν ἐπανελθεῖν, θεὸν δι᾿ ἐκείνας τὰς δυνάμεις ἑαυτὸν ἀναγορεύοντα. ἐγὼ δ᾿ οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως ἂν μάγος ἠγωνίσατο διδάξαι λόγον, πείθοντα πάντα πράττειν, ὡς θεοῦ κρίνοντος ἕκαστον ἐπὶ πᾶσι τοῖς πεπραγμένοις, καὶ ουτω διατιθέντα τοὺς ἑαυτοῦ μαθητὰς, οἷς ἔμελλε χρήσασθαι διακόνοις τῆς ἑαυτοῦ διδασκαλίας. ἆρα γὰρ κἀκεῖνοι οὕτω διδαχθέντες ποιεῖν δυνάμεις ᾕρουν τοὺς ἀκούοντας ἢ οὐδὲ δυνάμεις ἐποίουν; τὸ μὲν οὖν λέγειν ὅτι οὐδαμῶς δυνάμεις ἐποίουν ἀλλὰ πιστεύσαντες οὐδεμιᾷ λόγων ἱκανότητι παραπλησίως τῇ ἐν διαλεκτικῇ Ἑλλήνων σοφίᾳ ἐπέδωκαν ἑαυτοὺς τῷ καινὸν διδάσκειν λόγον οἷς ἂν ἐπιδημήσωσι πάνυ ἐστὶν ἄλογον· τίνι γὰρ θαῤῥοῦντες ἐδίδασκον τὸν λόγον καὶ ἐκαινοτόμουν; εἰ δὲ δυνάμεις ἐτέλουν κἀκεῖνοι, τίνα ἔχει πιθανότητα τὸ μάγους τοσούτοις κινδύνοις ἑαυτοὺς παραβεβληκέναι (διὰ) διδασκαλίαν μαγείας ἀπαγορεύουσαν;
pass_a_gloss: Further, having taken (λαβών) from the account (ἱστορία) written in the Gospel according to Matthew about Jesus' having gone abroad (ἀποδεδημηκέναι) to Egypt, he did not believe (οὐκ ἐπίστευσεν) the miraculous things (τὰ παράδοξα) regarding this, neither that an angel gave this as an oracle/command (ἔχρησεν), nor whether Jesus leaving Judea and sojourning (ἐπιδημῶν) in Egypt hinted at something (ᾐνίσσετο); but he fabricated (ἀνέπλασε) something else. Agreeing somehow (συγκατατιθέμενος πως) with the miraculous powers (δυνάμεις) which Jesus did, in which he persuaded the many to follow him as Christ, but wishing to slander (διαβάλλειν) them as having come about from magic (μαγεία) and not by divine power (θείᾳ δυνάμει); for he says that he, having been reared in obscurity/secretly (σκότιον τραφέντα), having worked for hire (μισθαρνήσαντα) into Egypt, having made trial of (πειραθέντα) certain powers, came back from there, proclaiming himself (ἀναγορεύοντα) God through those powers. But I do not know how a magician (μάγος) would have striven (ἠγωνίσατο) to teach a doctrine (λόγος) persuading [people] to do everything as of God judging (κρίνοντος) each one upon all the things done, and so disposing (διατιθέντα) his own disciples, whom he was going to use as ministers (διάκονοι) of his teaching. Did they too, thus taught to do powers, win over (ᾕρουν) the hearers, or did they not even do powers? To say they did no powers at all, but having believed (πιστεύσαντες), with no competence (ἱκανότητι) of words comparable to the dialectical (διαλεκτικῇ) wisdom of Greeks, they gave themselves to teaching a new doctrine (καινὸν λόγον) to those among whom they might sojourn, is altogether irrational (ἄλογον); for trusting (θαρροῦντες) in what did they teach the doctrine and innovate (ἐκαινοτόμουν)? But if they too performed powers, what plausibility (πιθανότης) has it that magicians exposed themselves (παραβεβληκέναι) to so many dangers for a teaching forbidding (ἀπαγορεύουσαν) magic?
pass_b_english: Next he takes the account written in the Gospel according to Matthew of Jesus' journey into Egypt (Matthew 2:13–15). He does not believe the miraculous part of it, either that an angel gave the command for it, or whether Jesus' leaving Judea and staying in Egypt hinted at some hidden meaning. Instead he has made up another story. In a way he grants the miraculous works that Jesus did, by which he persuaded the many to follow him as Christ; but he wants to slander them as done by magic and not by divine power. For he says that “he was brought up in obscurity, went to Egypt to work for hire, tried his hand there at certain powers, and came back from there proclaiming himself God on the strength of those powers.”

For my part, I do not know how a magician would have laboured to teach a doctrine that persuades people to do everything in the belief that God will judge each person for all that he has done, and that shapes in this way his own disciples, whom he meant to use as ministers of his teaching. Did they too, having been taught in this way to work miracles, win over those who heard them, or did they not work miracles at all? To say that they worked no miracles at all, but that, once they believed, they gave themselves to teaching a new doctrine to whomever they came among, without any skill in speech comparable to the dialectical wisdom of the Greeks, is wholly unreasonable. For in what did they trust when they taught the doctrine and brought in something new? But if they too performed miracles, what likelihood is there that magicians would have exposed themselves to such great dangers for a teaching that forbids magic?

choices.choice: Celsus's charge is in indirect speech in the Greek (accusative and infinitive after φησί); it is set in quotation marks as his reported words. σκότιον τραφέντα: 'brought up in obscurity'; σκότιος can also mean 'born in secret, illegitimate', which would fit the Panthera slander of 1.28 and 1.32, but the participle τραφέντα points to upbringing, so 'obscurity' is kept. μισθαρνήσαντα εἰς Αἴγυπτον picks up 1.28 (hired himself out in Egypt). 'God will judge each person for all that he has done' echoes the common teaching of judgment by deeds (compare Matthew 16:27; Romans 2:6; 2 Corinthians 5:10), but it is not a quotation, so no verse is cited inline. Koetschau's supplement (διά) before διδασκαλίαν is followed. καὶ οὕτω διατιθέντα (accusative) agrees with λόγον, πείθοντα: it is the doctrine that shapes the disciples. The staged text has ουτω without breathing; read οὕτω.
οὔτε εἴ τι ᾐνίσσετο rendered as 'or whether ... hinted at some hidden meaning' (was 'or that ... pointed to')
agency fixed: διατιθέντα (accusative) agrees with λόγον, so the doctrine, not the magician, shapes the disciples
